title: Classification of Vasculitis and Large Vessel Vasculitis

questions.sec: Vasculitis definition and Chapel-Hill vessel-size classification
questions.q: In the source definition, vasculitis is inflammation within the vessel wall that most directly leads to which two consequences?
opts: Low ESR/CRP with isolated fibrosis only
Raised ESR/CRP with ischemia and organ damage
questions.exp: Vasculitis is defined as vessel-wall inflammation, with raised ESR/CRP and ischemia or organ damage. (Book p491)

questions.sec: Vasculitis definition and Chapel-Hill vessel-size classification
questions.q: Which statement matches the source note on diagnosing vasculitis?
opts: There is no gold standard test and no diagnostic criteria
Temporal artery biopsy is a gold standard for every vasculitis
ANCA positivity alone is diagnostic of all vasculitis
questions.exp: The page explicitly notes no gold standard test to diagnose vasculitis and no diagnostic criteria. (Book p491)

questions.sec: Vasculitis definition and Chapel-Hill vessel-size classification
questions.q: A systemic-sclerosis patient has endothelial injury, thrombus formation, capillary hypoxia, myofibroblast activation, TGF-beta and fibrosis with low ESR/CRP. Which source term fits best?
questions.exp: The vasculopathy note uses systemic sclerosis as the example and lists endothelial injury through TGF-beta fibrosis with low ESR/CRP. (Book p491)

questions.sec: Vasculitis definition and Chapel-Hill vessel-size classification
questions.q: The revised Chapel Hill 2012 classification on this page is based mainly on what?
opts: Presence of granuloma in biopsy only
questions.exp: The classification criteria are the revised Chapel Hill consensus 2012 classification and are based on predominantly affected vessel size. (Book p491)

questions.sec: Vasculitis definition and Chapel-Hill vessel-size classification
questions.q: Which vessel-disease pairing belongs to the large-vessel row of the table?
opts: Aorta and branches: temporal or giant-cell arteritis and Takayasu arteritis
questions.exp: Large vessels are the aorta and its branches, with temporal/giant-cell arteritis and Takayasu arteritis listed. (Book p491)

questions.sec: Vasculitis definition and Chapel-Hill vessel-size classification
questions.q: Which list contains only ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitides as printed?
opts: PAN, Kawasaki disease and isolated aortitis
Behcet disease, Cogan syndrome and HUV
questions.exp: The ANCA-associated list contains GPA, allergic/eosinophilic GPA and microscopic polyangiitis. (Book p491)

questions.sec: Vasculitis definition and Chapel-Hill vessel-size classification
questions.q: Which list contains only immune-complex mediated small-vessel vasculitides on the page?
opts: Anti-GBM disease, HSP and cryoglobulinemia-associated vasculitis
questions.exp: The immune-complex mediated list includes anti-GBM disease, HSP and cryoglobulinemia-associated vasculitis. (Book p491)

questions.sec: Vasculitis definition and Chapel-Hill vessel-size classification
questions.q: Hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis is linked to which antibody and pathognomonic feature?
opts: Anti-PR3 antibody and saddle nose deformity
questions.exp: HUV is marked by anti-C1q antibody, SLE-overlap features and pathognomonic interface dermatitis. (Book p492)

questions.sec: Vasculitis definition and Chapel-Hill vessel-size classification
questions.q: The source names the most common vasculitis in adults worldwide and in children as which pair?
opts: Takayasu arteritis in adults and Kawasaki disease in children
PAN in adults and cryoglobulinemia in children
Behcet disease in adults and Cogan syndrome in children
Temporal/giant-cell arteritis in adults and HSP in children
questions.exp: The margin note states most common vasculitis: adults temporal/giant-cell arteritis worldwide, children HSP. (Book p492)

questions.sec: Vasculitis definition and Chapel-Hill vessel-size classification
questions.q: Which two disorders are listed under variable vessel vasculitis?
questions.exp: Variable vessel vasculitis consists of Behcet disease and Cogan syndrome in the printed list. (Book p492)

questions.sec: Vasculitis definition and Chapel-Hill vessel-size classification
questions.q: A biopsy-proven vasculitis is limited to skin capillaries/post-capillary venules. Which single-organ vasculitis example is printed?
questions.exp: Single-organ vasculitis examples list skin capillaries/post-capillary venules as cutaneous leukocytoclastic angiitis. (Book p492)

questions.sec: Vasculitis definition and Chapel-Hill vessel-size classification
questions.q: Which connective-tissue disease exception is paired with medium-vessel vasculitis in the source?
questions.exp: Among CTD-associated exceptions, RA and Sjogren are bracketed with medium-vessel vasculitis. (Book p492)

questions.sec: Vasculitis definition and Chapel-Hill vessel-size classification
questions.q: Which drug pair is specifically placed under ANCA-associated drug-induced small-vessel vasculitis?
questions.exp: Drug-induced ANCA-associated vasculitis lists hydralazine and propylthiouracil, while penicillins, sulfonamides and thiazides are immune-complex mediated. (Book p492)

questions.sec: Vasculitis definition and Chapel-Hill vessel-size classification
questions.q: A secondary infectious vasculitis is described as HCV-associated and cryoglobulinemia-like. Which source pairing is being applied?
questions.exp: The infection list pairs HCV with cryoglobulinemia-like vasculitis and HBV with PAN-like disease. (Book p492)

questions.sec: Vasculitis definition and Chapel-Hill vessel-size classification
questions.q: Malignancy-related secondary paraneoplastic vasculitis in the source primarily involves which vessels and malignancies?
opts: Small vessels; lymphoma, hairy-cell leukemia, bladder cancer and RCC
Large vessels; myeloma, melanoma and colon cancer
Medium vessels only; thyroid and ovarian cancers
questions.exp: Malignancy-related vasculitis is noted to involve small vessels and is associated with lymphoma, hairy-cell leukemia, bladder carcinoma and RCC. (Book p493)

questions.q: Which histology is shared by the large-vessel vasculitides in the source?
opts: Necrotizing inflammation without granuloma as the rule
Pure eosinophilic infiltrates without vessel-wall involvement
Transmural inflammation with lymphocytes/macrophages, granuloma and few giant cells in about 50%
Leukocytoclasis with immune-complex deposits in every case
questions.exp: Both large-vessel diseases have similar histology: transmural inflammation involving intima/media/adventitia, lymphocytes/macrophages, granuloma and few giant cells, seen in 50% cases. (Book p493)

questions.q: Which synonym and vessel pattern correctly fit giant cell arteritis?
opts: Pulseless disease involving only renal arteries
Middle aortic syndrome sparing temporal arteries
Cutaneous leukocytoclastic angiitis of post-capillary venules
Temporal/cranial/granulomatous arteritis involving extracranial vessels with internal elastic lamina
questions.exp: GCA synonyms are temporal arteritis, cranial arteritis and granulomatous arteritis; vessels are extracranial vessels with internal elastic lamina, sparing intracranial vessels. (Book p493)

questions.q: What age and sex pattern is printed for GCA?
opts: Presentation after 50 years, mean diagnosis 72 years, female:male 2:1
Presentation before 40 years, mean diagnosis 24 years, female:male 9:1
Middle age only, equal sex distribution
questions.exp: GCA presents after 50 years, mean age of diagnosis is 72 years and the female:male ratio is 2:1. (Book p493)

questions.q: Which order of artery involvement is printed as most common in GCA?
opts: Superficial temporal > vertebral > ophthalmic > posterior ciliary
questions.exp: The most common artery sequence in GCA is superficial temporal, then vertebral, ophthalmic and posterior ciliary. (Book p493)

questions.q: What is the printed GCA-PMR 50/20 rule?
opts: ESR 50 in 20% of all cases only
PMR symptoms in 50% of GCA cases and GCA symptoms in 20% of PMR cases
GCA in 50% of PMR cases and PMR in 20% of GCA cases
questions.exp: The GCA-PMR syndrome note states PMR symptoms occur in 50% of GCA cases and GCA symptoms occur in 20% of PMR cases. (Book p493)

questions.q: An older patient has early morning pain and stiffness of shoulder, hip and pelvic girdle with ESR above 50. Which source diagnosis is suggested and what is its key differential?
opts: Takayasu arteritis; differentiate from Kawasaki disease
Behcet disease; differentiate from SLE oral ulcers
questions.exp: PMR features are tendinitis/bursitis/enthesitis with early morning pain and stiffness in shoulder, hip and pelvic girdle, ESR >50, and differential diagnosis is late-onset RA. (Book p494)

questions.q: Which pathology pattern is printed for PMR?
opts: IL-6 predominant inflammation type and IFN-gamma mediated ischemia type
questions.exp: PMR pathology is listed as IL-6 predominant inflammation type and IFN-gamma mediated ischemia type. (Book p494)

questions.q: Which association list belongs to PMR/GCA in the source?
opts: Smoking, VZV isolated from biopsy with no role of acyclovir, HLA DRB1-04 and MICA A5
questions.exp: Associations include smoking, VZV isolated from biopsy with no role of acyclovir, and genetic HLA DRB1-04/MICA A5 allele. (Book p494)

questions.q: A patient over 50 has new recurrent boring headache of moderate-to-severe intensity. Which typical GCA feature is this?
opts: Headache: new onset, recurring, unusual type and boring pain
Jaw claudication from renal artery stenosis
questions.exp: Typical GCA headache is new onset, moderate-severe, recurring, unusual type and boring in nature. (Book p494)

questions.q: Which ESR statement matches the typical GCA page?
opts: ESR is irrelevant in GCA and PMR
ESR is usually above 100 mm/hr, while ACR uses above 50 mm/hr
questions.exp: The clinical-features page prints ESR >100 mm/hr and notes ACR >50 mm/hr. (Book p494)

questions.q: Jaw claudication with ophthalmoplegia is highlighted in GCA because it has what predictive value?
opts: It indicates HSP rather than arteritis
questions.exp: Jaw claudication due to maxillary artery involvement, along with ophthalmoplegia, is noted as 100% positive predictive value for GCA. (Book p494)

questions.q: Which atypical presentation is explicitly listed for GCA?
opts: Pyrexia of unknown origin in age over 50 years
questions.exp: Atypical GCA includes pyrexia of unknown origin in age over 50 years, cervical radiculopathy and recurrent throat pain/cough. (Book p495)

questions.q: For temporal artery biopsy in suspected GCA, what segment length is printed to overcome skip lesions?
questions.exp: Temporal artery biopsy is the investigation of choice, and a 4–6 cm long segment is taken to overcome skip lesions. (Book p495)

questions.q: Which color-Doppler performance and sign are printed for GCA?
opts: No Doppler role and no named sign
questions.exp: Color Doppler is listed with 70% sensitivity and 80% specificity; the halo sign is a hypoechoic area around the temporal artery in longitudinal and transverse sections. (Book p495)

questions.q: Which item is part of the ACR criteria for GCA?
questions.exp: ACR criteria shown are onset age >50, new localized headache, temporal artery tenderness or decreased pulsations, ESR ≥50 mm/hr and biopsy with transmural inflammation. (Book p495)

questions.q: What first-line GCA treatment dose is printed?
opts: Steroids 40–60 mg/day, about 1 mg/kg/day, then taper
questions.exp: Treatment lists steroids as first line, 40–60 mg/day or 1 mg/kg/day, tapered down. (Book p495)

questions.q: Tocilizumab is printed for GCA in what context?
opts: JAK inhibitor for best response under 3 months
Anti-IL-6 therapy for flares common on low-dose steroids with raised ESR
Anti-CD20 therapy for all first presentations
questions.exp: Tocilizumab is anti-IL-6 and is indicated for flares, especially common at low-dose steroids with increased ESR. (Book p495)

questions.q: Which synonym set belongs to Takayasu arteritis in the source?
opts: Temporal arteritis, cranial arteritis and granulomatous arteritis
Aortic arch syndrome, nonspecific aortoarteritis, occlusive thromboaortopathy, pulseless disease and middle aortic syndrome
questions.exp: Takayasu synonyms listed are aortic arch syndrome, nonspecific aortoarteritis, occlusive thromboaortopathy, pulseless disease and middle aortic syndrome. (Book p496)

questions.q: What demographic pattern is printed for Takayasu arteritis?
opts: Presentation below 40 years, mean diagnosis 24 years, female:male 9:1
Presentation after 50 years, mean diagnosis 72 years, female:male 2:1
questions.exp: Takayasu arteritis presents before 40 years, mean age of diagnosis 24 years, with female:male ratio 9:1. (Book p496)

questions.q: Which conditions are included in the note on female:male 9:1 ratio?
opts: Behcet disease and Cogan syndrome only
Sjogren, SLE, Takayasu, fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue syndrome and primary biliary cirrhosis
HSP, Kawasaki disease and pseudogout only
questions.exp: The 9:1 note lists Sjogren, SLE, Takayasu, fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue syndrome and primary biliary cirrhosis. (Book p496)

questions.q: Which two diseases are listed as having pulmonary artery involvement?
questions.exp: The note lists pulmonary artery involvement in Takayasu arteritis and Behcet disease. (Book p496)

questions.q: Which pathology/vessel pattern fits Takayasu arteritis?
opts: Anti-C1q with interface dermatitis and dermal capillaries only
Focal segmental necrosis with ANCA positivity
HLA-B52/B67, vessel-specific TLR expression, segmental stenosis more than aneurysm, subclavian artery most common
questions.exp: Takayasu pathology includes HLA-B52/B67, TLR expression differing by vessel, segmental stenosis more than aneurysm and subclavian artery as the most common vessel. (Book p496)

questions.q: A young woman with upper-limb claudication has unequal arm blood pressures differing by more than 10 mmHg and abdominal/carotid/aortic/femoral bruits. Which source disease fits?
questions.exp: Takayasu clinical features include upper-extremity claudication, pulse inequality, unequal arm BP >10 mmHg and abdominal/carotid/aortic/femoral bruits. (Book p496)

questions.q: Which item is included in ACR classification criteria for Takayasu arteritis?
questions.exp: Takayasu ACR criteria include onset <40 years, limb claudication, decreased brachial artery pulse, unequal arm BP >10 mmHg, subclavian/aortic bruit and angiographic stenosis. (Book p497)

questions.q: Which investigation is listed as IOC for Takayasu diagnosis and follow-up and best for vessel-wall thickness?
questions.exp: MR angiography is IOC for diagnosis and follow-up and gives the best measure of vessel wall thickness. (Book p497)

questions.q: When is conventional angiography used in Takayasu arteritis according to the page?
opts: It is the first investigation for every patient
It is the gold standard and is done if vessel intervention is planned
questions.exp: Conventional angiography is marked gold standard and done if vessel intervention is planned. (Book p497)

questions.q: Which Takayasu treatment list is printed before the summary table?
opts: Steroids as DOC, tocilizumab, and percutaneous transluminal renal angiogram with stenting
Supportive care only because it is self-limiting
questions.exp: Treatment lists steroids as DOC, tocilizumab and percutaneous transluminal renal angiogram with stenting. (Book p498)

questions.q: Which summary-table feature favors Takayasu arteritis rather than temporal arteritis?
opts: Female:male ratio 9:1 with age under 40 years
questions.exp: Takayasu shows F:M 9:1, age <40 years, average onset 25 years and Asian highest incidence; temporal arteritis has visual loss 10–30%, average age 72 and Scandinavian incidence. (Book p498)

questions.q: Which summary-table feature favors temporal arteritis rather than Takayasu arteritis?
opts: Visual loss 10–30% and aorta/major branches in one-third of cases
questions.exp: Temporal arteritis has visual loss 10–30%, one-third aorta/major branch involvement, rare renal HTN/claudication and rare need for surgical intervention. (Book p498)
